passage: At the temple fair Kashish begged for a second jalebi, and her father, Sachin, shook his head. "No, beta. You had one." Her face crumpled. "You are mean! I hate you!" The words flew out, and then her stomach turned over as she saw his face. She pressed herself against his leg and hid her eyes. Sachin crouched down and said gently, "You are angry, and I still love you." Kashish sniffed and looked up, a little frightened, and he wiped her cheek.

qa.q: What did Kashish ask for at the temple fair?
qa.a: She begged for a second jalebi.

qa.q: Why did Kashish hide her eyes after she said "I hate you"?
qa.a: She was angry, but she was also afraid of what she had said and that it might change her father's love.

qa.q: What did Sachin say that helped Kashish, and why?
qa.a: He said, "You are angry, and I still love you." That teaches her hard words do not end love, so she can settle.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel when Kashish shouts that he is mean?
qa.a: It probably stings, but he sees a small child who is upset. He stays gentle so that she knows he is not going away.

grounding: I say you are mean, I hate you and feel angry and afraid; a parent replies you are angry, I still love you.

passage: At the swimming club, the whistle blew for the end of the lesson. "Out now, Tanvir," his dad, Farhan, called from the edge. "No! You're mean! I hate you!" Tanvir shouted, splashing. Then his eyes went wide. He climbed out and stood dripping, not looking up. Farhan wrapped him in the big towel. "You're angry. I still love you." Tanvir's chin wobbled. "Even when I said hate?" "Even then." In the changing room, Tanvir leaned against his dad's arm while his hair was dried.

qa.q: What did Farhan wrap Tanvir in?
qa.a: Farhan wrapped him in the big towel.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's eyes go wide after he shouted?
qa.a: He felt afraid of what he had said, worried that his hard words might end his dad's love, while still feeling angry.

qa.q: What did Farhan's reply teach Tanvir?
qa.a: By saying "You're angry. I still love you," he showed that hard words do not end love, without shouting back.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Tanvir says he hates him?
qa.a: It may sting, but Farhan understands it is anger talking, so he stays warm and steady.

grounding: A child shouts "I hate you" at a parent's no and feels scared by it, and the parent answers with calm love.

passage:
Tuesday: Maa said no to the park because of homework time. Usha yelled, "You're mean! I hate you!" and ran to her room. Under her blanket, she felt hot and shaky.
Wednesday: At breakfast, Usha would not look at Anirban, her father. He sat beside her. "You were angry yesterday. I still love you. So does Maa." Usha peeked out. "Even after hate?" "Even after."
Saturday: Maa said no to more ice cream. Usha scowled. "I'm angry at you." Then she hugged Maa's leg anyway.

qa.q: Why did Maa say no to the park on Tuesday?
qa.a: Maa said no because it was homework time.

qa.q: How was Usha feeling under her blanket?
qa.a: She felt angry and afraid at the same time, hot and shaky about the hard words she had shouted.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped?
qa.a: He sat beside Usha, named her anger and told her they both still loved her, so she learned hard words do not end love.

qa.q: How does Maa probably see Usha's hug on Saturday?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and relieved, seeing Usha can say she is angry and still stay close.

grounding: Over several days, a child learns that saying hard words in anger does not end her parents' love.
